prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I have not changed my preferred configuration: a single-part B001 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Having read the whole first-round exchange, I tested it again against the strongest objections, not against the head count. The chain from proglucagon-derived peptide biology, through human demonstration that GLP-1 is a glucose-dependent incretin (Holst), identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form (Mojsov), and the receptor and gut-hormone biology with the therapeutic concept (Drucker), to randomized outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal endpoints, is the most complete mechanism-to-medicine arc on the shortlist. It is original, independently confirmed over decades and mature. Of the supplied configurations, no other has a comparable combination of mechanistic clarity, demonstrated benefit and a laureate set that fits the three-person limit. I would word the citation around physiology and the identity of the active peptide, and name type 2 diabetes and obesity, since the outcome evidence now covers both.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the real weakness, and round 2 has not removed it. The early peptide-identification priority between Mojsov and the Habener group is not settled by the supplied evidence, and several of us, myself included, rely on recollection for the chronology. Knudsen is omitted, and that is a judgement that the prize recognises discovery of the physiology and the active peptide, not the engineering of durable analogues. It is a cost and not a finding that development work is lesser. If Mojsov's priority were shown to be materially weaker than the record we have, the third name would be open to revision. I do not have that evidence, and the discipline is to say so and not assume it. A smaller concern is that long-term safety of chronic use is still being characterised, which does not bear on the core discovery.

responses.point: The chair reads Knudsen's analogue work as an extension of an already-established mechanism and would keep her out, while recording that her case deserves a hearing under a drug-development framing.
responses.response: I accept the chair's reading as a defensible basis for the trio, and in round 1 I underplayed how much of the case rests on that reading. Where I still differ is the weight. Durable analogues are why the physiology reached patients, so the exclusion should be recorded as a judgement and not presented as obvious. I do not propose to replace any of the three, because I can find no documented ground to say one of them has a weaker claim than the others on discovery. On the chair's question about wording, I prefer naming both type 2 diabetes and obesity, because the outcome evidence supports both and the citation should not look narrower than the discovery.

responses.point: Marie says the early peptide-identification priority is the one point that could change her view of the trio, and that the citation should anchor on physiology and the active peptide and not on a drug.
responses.response: I agree on both points and I share her uncertainty. The evidence supplied to us does not settle Mojsov against Habener, so I am voting on the described contribution, which is identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and not on a priority claim I cannot check. Her point also shows why the citation wording matters. Writing it as the identification of the active form, as a physiological finding, avoids claiming sole first discovery. If the committee preferred to hedge, I would accept a citation that stays on physiology and the active form without saying who found it first.

responses.point: Thomas holds that a single-achievement GLP-1 prize is the cleanest allocation but says that, if credit cannot be settled, B043 or B045 could be easier to defend, and he asks whether a second part would be worthwhile.
responses.response: I considered a two-part configuration seriously. Pairing B001 with B045 or B043 would force B001 down to one or two names, and no member has shown a documented ground for dropping Drucker, Holst or Mojsov. A second part would trade a known attribution cost for a different one. For B045 the cost is Eshhar and Gross, and Rosenberg's place, and for B043 the clinical consequences are still emerging. I would also not hold B001 to a standard of settled credit that no shortlisted candidate meets. The B001 credit questions are real but bounded, so I keep a single part. I would revisit this if B001 stalled, and B045 would be my next choice.

responses.point: Sten would narrow B045 to June and Sadelain and exclude Rosenberg, and treats the missing Eshhar credit as a serious gap, while listing B043 as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the Eshhar and Gross gap is a serious problem for B045 and that June and Sadelain is the tighter core. Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer work looks to me like a related but distinct achievement, so putting him inside the same claim blurs the attribution. That is why I keep B045 as an alternative and not as a co-equal second part. I also keep B004 over B043 as my second alternative. B043 has the cleanest names, but the physiological and clinical consequences of the UPR are still emerging, and the evidence of benefit is firmer for BCR-ABL inhibition, even though Perlmann's objection that the prize would read as a drug award is fair.

responses.point: Rickard sees the B039 optogenetics credit as hard to split and does not treat limited clinical translation as disqualifying for B043, and she shares the view that the Eshhar gap is a serious one for CAR-T.
responses.response: As a neuroscientist I agree on B039. The six-name credit set against a three-person cap has no split I could defend as non-arbitrary, so I will not move it up merely because I use the tools. On B043 I concede her point in part. Limited translation is not a disqualifier for a foundational mechanism, and I would not hold it against Mori and Walter in a later year. My reservation is about this year, not about merit, because B001 has demonstrated population-scale benefit and a workable laureate set. I also share her concern on the Eshhar gap, which keeps B045 behind B001.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's credit for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide relative to the Habener group would hold up under primary evidence, which the supplied record does not provide
Whether excluding Knudsen is acceptable to the committee or whether a swap of one name is preferable, and on what documented ground
Whether B045 can be given a defensible laureate set without Eshhar and Gross, and whether Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy work is a distinct achievement from the engineered CAR-T claim
Whether the committee would accept the same B001 trio if the citation were drafted in a narrower form that avoids any statement of who identified the active peptide first
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented involvement with any credited name on the shortlist. I have a 2009 co-authored paper with fellow committee member Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, which is unrelated to any shortlisted ballot, and I have co-authored work with Sten Grillner and Patrik Ernfors, who are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I do not request recusal.
